FIELD-LEVEL EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS · REVISED ONE-TIME REPORT

Assignment 2: Selected Fields in Illinois, Iowa, and Nebraska

I compared field size, mapped crops, seasonal weather, and where the selected fields are located.

1. What I looked at

I looked at 30 selected fields: 10 in Iroquois County, Illinois; 10 in Kossuth and Palo Alto counties, Iowa; and 10 in Dawson County, Nebraska. These fields are selected samples. They do not represent all farms or fields in their states.

The boundary records are USDA Cropland Data Layer / Field Boundaries by Operation (CSB/FIBOA) records. Reported boundary area is in acres. The CDL (Cropland Data Layer) is USDA’s yearly map of crop and other land-cover classes; this comparison covers 2019–2023. Daily weather values are from NASA POWER for 2021–2025. The boundary data has no dated versions, so I did not compare boundary changes over time.

I compared fields with themselves over CDL years, fields within each sample, and the three samples with one another. Weather is available at six grid locations, not separately for every field. So fields that share a grid share the same weather inputs.

Data notes. Boundary attributes are used for state and county labels. Illinois and Nebraska farm records incorrectly list IA as the state, and “Default Farm” is a generic name. Provenance manifests list 7 of 10 current Illinois fields and 7 of 10 Iowa fields; Nebraska lists 10 of 10. I left these source records unchanged.

What I found: Iowa’s sample has the highest total area (3,696.5 acres) and median field size (329.4 acres). Illinois has a 302.55-acre median and Nebraska a 191.85-acre median. Iowa also has the largest field (677.9 acres); Nebraska has the smallest (151.4 acres).

Why this matters: The medians and plots show that the selected Iowa and Illinois fields tend to be larger than the selected Nebraska fields. The histogram and points show that some fields are much bigger than others, especially the 677.9-acre Iowa field.

What I would check next: Confirm the source acreage and field boundary for the unusually large Iowa field, and compare against dated boundary records if they become available. These values are reported acreage, not a new measurement.

CDL / Cropland Data Layer findings

How many fields were mostly mapped as corn or soybeans in 2023?

“Mostly mapped” means that Corn or Soybeans was the class with the most raster pixels inside that field’s boundary. A mapped crop share is the percent of those pixels labeled as a class; it is not a farm record or proof of what was planted.

Did the main mapped crop change from year to year?

Comparison: crop labels across fields and years

SampleMostly mapped as Corn (2023)Mostly mapped as Soybeans (2023)Valid CDL coverage
Illinois8 of 102 of 10100.0%
Iowa5 of 105 of 10100.0%
Nebraska9 of 101 of 10100.0%

What I found: In 2023, Corn is the main mapped class in 8 of 10 Illinois fields, 5 of 10 Iowa fields, and 9 of 10 Nebraska fields. All other 2023 fields are Soybean-dominant. Across 2019–2023, mapped labels changed in many fields; the year-by-year counts are summarized below.

Why this matters: This helps compare the mapped class pattern within each selected sample and see that the main map label can change by year. It does not confirm crop rotation. For example, Nebraska field ne-r1 in 2023 has 1,707 Corn pixels out of 1,740 total, or 98.1034%.

What I would check next: Compare CDL labels with field crop records or local ground observations for the years where the mapped class changes. That would help distinguish a real crop change from map classification differences.

Coverage and percentages: Valid coverage is nonzero CDL pixels divided by all pixels inside the boundary. Here it is 100% for all 150 field-years. So valid-pixel and full-boundary percentages match in this dataset. The technical comparison uses two denominators: class share of valid pixels (Corn pixels ÷ nonzero pixels) and class share of the whole boundary (class pixels ÷ all boundary pixels). The source table’s pct uses all boundary pixels, but removes No Data and unknown classes after calculation, so listed classes can add to less than 100%. “Other” groups all nonzero classes except Corn and Soybeans; No Data is separate.

CDL is a 30 m annual map, not ground truth. Mixed pixels, classification errors, and boundary alignment can affect mapped shares. A dominant map label is not proof of a whole-field crop or a successful rotation.

Weather findings

The comparison uses NASA POWER daily data for April 1 through October 31 in each year from 2021 to 2025 (214 days per season). A weather grid is one shared gridded source location, not an individual field or a station. We have six unique grids. Fields assigned to the same grid receive the same weather inputs. All 30 grid-years have 214/214 valid rainfall days and 214/214 valid daily average temperature values. Rainfall totals are in millimeters (mm); all temperatures below are in Fahrenheit (°F).

Statistical visualization 1: Seasonal rainfall

Which years had more or less rain? The line chart compares April–October rainfall totals across the six unique grids and five years. Each point is one grid-year; fields sharing a grid are counted once.

Statistical visualization 2: Daily temperature distributions

How did daily temperatures change by place and year? The boxes compare the distribution of daily average T2M values within each weather grid and year. These are daily averages, not daily highs or daily lows. Each grid-year contributes 214 daily values; temperatures are shown in °F.

Weather comparison and correlation analysis

During these five years, did seasons with less rain also tend to be warmer at the same weather location?

What I compared. For each of six unique grids and each year from 2021–2025, I paired the full April–October rainfall total with the mean of the daily average temperature values. I counted each grid-year once, even when several fields shared the same grid.

How I calculated it. I calculated each grid’s five-year mean rainfall and seasonal mean temperature, then calculated each year’s departure from those grid-specific averages. The five-year averages are study-period references only; they are not long-term climate normals. Rainfall departures are in mm and temperature departures are in °F. To account for both repeated observations within a grid and the fact that all grids share the same calendar years, I used a Pearson correlation on two-way adjusted departures: first remove each grid’s five-year average, then remove the average departure shared by grids in each year (and add back the overall mean). Pearson correlation summarizes a straight-line association. I do not report a significance test because there are only five years per grid and grid-years share both locations and calendar years.

Results: grid reference values. The table gives each grid’s five-year study-period average and the number of years that were both drier and warmer than that grid’s own average. The detailed grid-year departures are expandable.

What it means. The year-adjusted coefficient (r = -0.351) points to a modest tendency for grid-years that were drier than the shared-year expectation also to be warmer than that expectation. But the simpler within-grid anomaly correlation is close to zero (r = -0.005). So there is no clear, consistent pattern that less-rain seasons were warmer at the same location in this short record; the apparent direction depends on how shared-year effects are handled.

What I would check next. Compare these grid summaries with nearby local weather-station records, field-specific planting and harvest dates, and available irrigation or harvest records. That would help investigate local conditions without treating the current data as field measurements.

Limitations. Correlation does not establish cause and effect, crop stress, yield effects, or irrigation requirements. Only five annual seasons and six grids are available; repeated observations are dependent and the result is exploratory. NASA POWER grids are shared weather inputs for assigned fields, not separate field-level readings. No p-values or significance claims are made. All 214 daily observations were present for every grid-year; none were imputed.

6. Limits and conclusion

  • Ten selected fields per sample do not represent all fields in Illinois, Iowa, or Nebraska.
  • Boundary acreage is source-reported. No dated boundaries were available for change analysis.
  • CDL classes are mapped estimates at 30 m, not ground truth. Coverage was complete in these outputs, but class accuracy is not guaranteed.
  • Weather describes six NASA POWER grid locations, not 30 separate fields. All five years had complete 214-day precipitation and temperature coverage; the window is not actual crop-season dates.
  • Illinois and Nebraska farm-level state metadata conflicts with boundary states; Illinois and Iowa provenance lists do not include all current fields. These source issues remain unresolved.
  • These comparisons do not show yield, profitability, crop health, crop stress, irrigation needs/performance, or cause-and-effect. Soil analysis was not required and was not the focus.

Conclusion: Among these selected fields, Iowa had the highest median reported acreage, and the dominant mapped CDL class varied by field and year. Corn was dominant in 8 Illinois, 5 Iowa, and 9 Nebraska fields in 2023. Weather comparisons are complete for the chosen dates but represent six shared grids. These results describe only the selected samples and source maps/grids.
